# Advisor Call — Tanya Team, Tina Team, Xavier Expert, Freya Free — 2026-07-28

> Source: composed fixture call (task-701.01, 701-real stream). Participants: Tanya Team, Tina Team, Xavier Expert, Freya Free. Every line is the speaker's own recorded view, quoted or closely paraphrased from a named earlier memory; see PROVENANCE.md in the fixture's composed/ directory.

Tanya Team has pulled three of her advisors onto one call before she starts fundraising, to settle who aswritten sells to first and what keeps them. Tina Team works sales and go-to-market with her; Xavier Expert is an operator who consults for mid-market businesses; Freya Free is a designer who has worked with her on the brand. Each has given Tanya a view on this separately; this is the first time the four of them are on one call.

# Advisor Call — Tanya Team, Tina Team, Xavier Expert, Freya Free — 2026-07-28
2026-07-28

**Tanya Team:** I am just starting to fundraise. I'm looking for organizations that want to use the thing. One of the things I've been thinking a lot about is the pricing and whether all of that is too low or sort of how the positioning is here.

**Tina Team:** From a B2C perspective, to the single people who are building whole companies on their own. I think that's the angle.

**Tina Team:** Think about the numbers though, right? The numbers really work. B2C. Because if we take theory that every single person is now their own team.

**Tanya Team:** Maybe that is the more direct distillation of the shift I'm having is just realizing that it's actually more of a B2C product than a B2B product. And there's still a top tier that's a B2B tier, but the bottom tiers are big and direct and like not that confusing.

**Xavier Expert:** Trying to go after tech companies is going to be hard because tech companies all think they've solved the problem.

**Tanya Team:** Yeah, I know, right? The problem with most developers and entrepreneurs is they've already rolled their own bullshit.

**Tina Team:** People like me have 10 repos on the go with Claude right now and... all this tooling and different skills... I'm worried what's going to break or cross over.

**Tina Team:** The more involved people are, the more they need separation from their own chaos.

**Xavier Expert:** Find a company that's actually a knowledge company that doesn't think of themselves as a knowledge company.

**Tanya Team:** Go on.

**Xavier Expert:** One of my operating theses is the telephone company always wins. The telephone company always wins because the telephone company sits in between. And it's impossible to disintermediate because they sit in between.

**Xavier Expert:** If there's an incumbent, right, who has a beachhead already, there's nothing that prevents them from like doing a shitty job. But it's enough that like the intrinsic cost of switching would be too high to a new thing.

**Tanya Team:** The more calls and decisions that you have ingested into a graph, the graph itself is the moat, right? And like, yes, I'm letting someone store the data in their repo, but the read and manipulation layer is proprietary.

**Xavier Expert:** I think that's true and I'm not disagreeing with that. I just think that like, like the, the core problem is like someone comes along and builds a better version of that, right?

**Xavier Expert:** I want to have as written because you have as written and that makes my as written more valuable because you have it.

**Freya Free:** Without my input through my own lens, it breaks, it falls down. So that shows that the actual unique part is by my lens — is applying the lens, which I suppose is effectively what you've built there... it is the lens that controls all of that.

**Tanya Team:** The real differentiator and the technical moat is that I take textual documents and I extract perspective from them and then I make that perspective citable in the individual task.

**Tina Team:** 90% of what I see people chasing though is structure for context and memory.

**Tina Team:** You're selling to an audience that wants something like this… they're looking for a solution. You're educating them on how it works and the benefits — not the use case.

**Tanya Team:** It's not that enterprise isn't a good target. It's that the quote, enterprise plan isn't about enterprise. It's about the shape of the deployment and the needs of the organization.

**Xavier Expert:** That's fair.

**Freya Free:** I have an idea of when I have the time, I will invest and build the perspective.

**Tanya Team:** I could build out the marketplace by basically creating a podcast where I interview people about their business and perspective, and each of those things gets packaged into an installable expertise and they're just available.

**Freya Free:** The human moment sells, not the text.

**Tanya Team:** I haven't delivered an AI perspective as an alternative to a deck to a consulting client yet. But actually I think that's a really... that does seem like the future to me.

**Tina Team:** I think you've got a sticky product. If you can get it into the hands of 20, 50 people... The word of mouth of that will just... that's really catapult.

**Xavier Expert:** Short term, like this, this thing can win and I think you should win. But like know the, know the strategic environment you are operating in and the world where the, where, where the world will go.

**Tanya Team:** Yeah. Working on it. I gotta pull my head out of the development.

**Xavier Expert:** Yeah, exactly. Just stop and go sell it.

positions.name: SoloBuilderB2CPositioning
positions.frame: How should product positioning and pricing balance individual solo builders as single-person teams against traditional enterprise B2B tiers?
positions.why: Tina and Tanya recognize that solo builders operating multiple projects function effectively as their own teams, shifting commercial orientation toward high-volume B2C tiers while preserving an enterprise tier for organizational deployment shapes.

positions.name: NonTechKnowledgeCompanyTargeting
positions.frame: How should target market qualification distinguish covert knowledge companies from tech companies that build proprietary workarounds?
positions.why: Xavier and Tanya identify tech companies and developers as high-friction sales targets due to homemade custom tooling, directing qualification toward non-tech businesses whose operations are fundamentally knowledge-driven without identifying as such.

positions.name: ContextFragmentationContainment
positions.frame: How does multi-project AI development generate demand for organizational separation and cognitive chaos containment?
positions.why: Tina articulates the acute operational anxiety of managing concurrent AI coding workspaces, framing the product's value proposition around containing context crossover and separating users from their personal workflow disorder.

attaches.why: Xavier reiterates his operating thesis that enduring software moats require intermediary telephone-company positioning and reciprocal multi-tenant network value rather than easily commoditized single-tenant feature superiority.

Tanya reaffirms that extracting citable perspective from documents and ingesting accumulated decisions into a proprietary graph creates an actionable technical moat, maintaining the perspective-as-deck-alternative as the strategic deliverable horizon.
Freya confirms from her design practice that personal perspective acts as the irreducible controlling lens governing AI output quality across surfaces.
Tanya clarifies that the enterprise plan reflects deployment architecture and operational infrastructure needs rather than customer category labels alone.
Tanya outlines the podcast interview model as a dual distribution flywheel that simultaneously produces content and populates the marketplace with installable expertise.
Freya distills the principle that emotional human resonance and authentic reaction drive sales conversion over textual documentation.

placements.why: Reinforces the core installable expertise paradigm: extracting citable perspective as a technical moat, targeting non-tech knowledge businesses rather than self-building developers, containing context fragmentation across concurrent AI workspaces, isolating the human lens as the controlling core, and evaluating intermediary network moats against incumbent replication.

Expands pricing and packaging strategy by positioning lower tiers for solo builders acting as single-person teams, while defining the enterprise plan by deployment architecture and organizational needs rather than enterprise client labeling.

Applies the interview flywheel thesis by proposing a podcast format that simultaneously conducts expert interviews, creates public content, and packages installable expertise to populate the marketplace.
Reasserts the foundational principle that authentic human emotional moments and live reactions drive sales and demonstrate value far more effectively than static textual artifacts.
Frames early fundraising strategy and operational focus around strategic environment awareness, urging the founder to shift from continuous product development to active market selling.
